chunks: And Muḥammad ibn Ja‘far al-Razzāz narrated to me from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusain ibn Abī al-Khaṭṭāb, from Mūsā ibn Sa‘dān, from ‘Abdillāh ibn Qāsim, from ‘Umar ibn Abān al-Kalbī, from Abān ibn Taghlib, who said:

Abū ‘Abdillāh (peace be upon him) said: Four thousand angels came down, intending to fight with al-Ḥusain ibn ‘Alī (peace be upon him), but permission was not granted to them to fight. So they returned to seek permission, and then came down, but al-Ḥusain (peace be upon him) had already been killed. They are by his grave, disheveled and covered with dust, weeping for him until the Day of Judgment. Their chief is an angel named al-Manṣūr.
ai.seo_question: Who are the angels weeping at the grave of Imam al-Husain (a.s.)?
ai.summary: Imam al-Ṣādiq (peace be upon him) narrates that four thousand angels descended to fight alongside al-Ḥusain ibn ‘Alī (peace be upon him) on the day of ‘Āshūrā but were not permitted to do so. After al-Ḥusain was killed, these angels remained by his grave, weeping for him until the Day of Judgment, with their chief being the angel al-Manṣūr. This tradition highlights the cosmic significance of the Battle of Karbala, illustrating that the tragedy was not merely a historical event but a celestial drama where the heavens themselves mourned the martyrdom of the Imam, reinforcing the Shia belief in the spiritual interconnection between the earthly and heavenly realms.
